slides.label: Projective Spaces: One Incidence Language
slides.notes: Open the lecture by treating the chapter as a change of language. The goal is not to add more coordinates, but to decide which coordinate changes should be invisible. The source span gives the route: rays, charts, incidence, projective maps, and perspective geometry.

slides.label: Homogeneous Points: Rays Not Coordinates
slides.notes: Emphasize that a homogeneous vector is a representative, not the point itself. Students should look at a whole ray through the origin and ask what survives rescaling. The answer is incidence with other linear objects, while length and chosen coordinates disappear.

slides.label: A Chart Is A Cut Through Rays
slides.notes: Use the chart picture to separate two acts. First the projective point is the ray. Then a chart cuts the ray and records ordinary numbers. Moving the cut changes the numbers, so the coordinate value is useful but not the geometric object.

slides.label: Topology And The Projective Line
slides.notes: This is where topology enters gently. The quotient says that nearby directions should define nearby projective points, and a chart supplies ordinary coordinates only where one selected coordinate is nonzero. The point at infinity is not an extra afterthought; it is another direction.

slides.label: Incidence From Linear Subspaces
slides.notes: Connect projective subspaces back to linear algebra. A projective line in the plane is a two-dimensional linear subspace upstairs. Incidence questions are therefore span and intersection questions before any drawing begins, which is why projective geometry feels algebraic.

slides.label: Projective Frames And Coordinates
slides.notes: A projective frame is the device that prevents coordinates from floating freely. In the plane, four points in general position let a projective map be pinned down up to scale. Stress that general position is doing real work here, because collinear choices cannot determine a full plane map.

slides.label: Projective Maps: Matrices Mod Scalars
slides.notes: Treat a projective transformation as a linear map with the scalar ambiguity removed. Multiplying the matrix by a nonzero constant changes representatives but not projective points. The important test is that lines go to lines and incidence relations are preserved.

slides.label: Cross-Ratio: A One-Dimensional Invariant
slides.notes: The cross-ratio is the small invariant that makes the one-dimensional theory concrete. Raw chart coordinates move under a fractional linear map, but this four-point number remains fixed. That is the habit the notebook asks for: inspect the invariant, not the displayed coordinates.

slides.label: Perspective: Parallel Lines Acquire A Point
slides.notes: Use the perspective image to make the payoff visible. Parallel affine lines are not sacred projective objects; after projection their images can share a vanishing point. What survives is collinearity and incidence with the image plane, not Euclidean parallelism.

slides.label: Camera-Like Projection As Matrix
slides.notes: Frame the camera model as projective geometry wearing applied notation. A world point and an image point are homogeneous vectors related by a rank three matrix. Depth is sacrificed, but incidences such as lines mapping to lines remain the reliable evidence.

slides.label: Pitfalls: Coordinates, Charts, Drawings
slides.notes: Pause on these pitfalls before the recap because they cause most computational mistakes. A tuple may name a point in one chart and fail in another. A drawing can suggest Euclidean facts that projective maps do not preserve, so every claim needs the right invariant.

slides.label: Recap: Tests For Projective Thinking
slides.notes: Close with a reusable checklist for the rest of the course. Projective thinking means choosing representatives late, checking incidence first, asking which chart is active, and measuring quantities such as cross-ratio only when they are meant to survive the transformation.
